  • Gianni Infantino is facing a battle to cling onto his Fifa presidency heading into next year’s election after his botched bid to sell off stakes in the World Cup to private investors resulted in a significant loss in support.
  • England and Wales have been among the football associations to join European governing body Uefa in leading the charge for Infantino’s removal from power, formally withdrawing their endorsement of the Swiss-Italian for re-election in March 2027.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Gianni Infantino is facing a battle to cling onto his Fifa presidency heading into next year’s election after his botched bid to sell off stakes in the World Cup to private investors resulted in a significant loss in support.

England and Wales have been among the football associations to join European governing body Uefa in leading the charge for Infantino’s removal from power, formally withdrawing their endorsement of the Swiss-Italian for re-election in March 2027.

Industry observers note that but as the dust has settled on his privatisation ploy, Infantino’s bid for a third term has strengthened. His allies have surfaced, with the likes of Mexico and Argentina joining Caf, the African football governing body, in reaffirming support for the under-fire president, and now the Asian Football Confederation (AFC) has reversed its position and backed Infantino with AFC president Sheikh Salman bin Ibrahim Al Khalifa underlining that there is “a true understanding between us”.

Recent findings suggest that infantino does have his challengers, with French Football Federation president Philippe Diallo, former Switzerland captain Ramon Vega and Japan Football Association honorary president Kozo Tashima all joining the race. The deadline to submit presidential bids is Wednesday 18 November.

But Infantino, confident of staying on for a fourth term, laughed in response to a question over whether he had considered resigning as president, declaring he retains the support of the “vast, vast majority” of world football.

Recent findings suggest that infantino needs 106 votes from the 211 member associations to be re-elected as president. Here is every country and confederation to have expressed their opposition or support for Infantino:.

According to recent reports, uefa, the governing body for Europe, has staunchly opposed Infantino’s leadership. They threatened a boycott of Fifa competitions before Infantino’s eventual climbdown but has continued to assert that his position is untenable, even taking legal action against the Swiss-Italian.

The body points to how there have not been “assurances” that attempts like the privatisation of the World Cup “to disfigure the game in this way will never be made again”.

It has been revealed that uefa general secretary Theodore Theodoridis has written to his Fifa counterpart Mattias Grafstrom setting out a series of questions on behalf of European members of the Fifa Council, demanding documents covering a series of Infantino controversies. Fifa has until 2 November to answer these questions.

Concacaf, the Confederation for North America and the Caribbean, came out in opposition of Infantino after being left stunned at the lack of consultation during the Fifa sell-off initiative, which they went on to reject.

After the blueprint was aborted, the confederation mentioned: “This recent unilateral and egregious act of poor governance and leadership follows a pattern of missteps and similar behaviour. A comprehensive reckoning with this presidency is imperative.”.

Concacaf president Victor Montagliani was initially seen as a front-runner to challenge Infantino in next March’s election but he now looks set to pursue another term as Concacaf chief.

The Albanian Football Federation aligned itself with Uefa.

“The Albanian Football Association has sent an official letter to Fifa Secretary General Mattias Grafström, informing him that it has withdrawn its support for Mr Gianni Infantino’s candidacy for another four-year term as Fifa President,” the statement confirmed.

Rinse and repeat for Austria’s federation, who remarked “a united approach by the European associations sends a strong signal of responsibility for the sport and of solidarity.”.

Industry observers note that belgium, who felt the brunt of another Infantino controversy at the World Cup over Folarin Balogun’s red card, have withdrawn their support for his re-election. citing Fifa’s failure to demonstrate “any transparency” under his leadership.

As did the Croatian Football Federation (HNS): "The Croatian Football Federation has informed Fifa of its decision to withdraw the support previously expressed for Mr Gianni Infantino's candidature for another term as Fifa president.

"This decision followed a thorough reassessment within the federation in light of recent developments surrounding the Fifa World Cup 2026 and discussions within our governing bodies. We consider our position to be clearly communicated to Fifa and have no further comment to add at this time.".

The Cyprus Football Association (CFA) aligned itself with Uefa’s position and said it felt Infantino could no longer continue as president.

"Under the weight of what has taken place and under today's conditions, the CFA finds that the necessary prerequisites are no longer in place for the President of Fifa to continue exercising his duties," the association mentioned.

Denmark did not endorse Infantino’s re-election bid prior to the scheme’s reveal and haven’t changed their stance.

There is also a precedent for their opposition to Infantino, with federation president Jesper Moller not supporting his re-election efforts back in 2022: “There is only one candidate ... but Denmark will not be supporting the current president.”.

The English FA is one of many European member associations to send a letter to Fifa withdrawing its support for Infantino’s re-election in 2027.

Infantino’s apology letter changed nothing for the FA, who was “deeply concerned about the lack of process and governance” surrounding his sell-off scheme.

It has been revealed that all the Nordic nations ended up joining forces in a combined statement, to say they had “lost confidence” in Infantino’s leadership. This included the Faroe Islands.

Finland kickstarted the process of formal withdrawals, with it being revealed that the Scandinavian member association was the first to send a letter officially withdrawing support for Infantino.

France withdrew their endorsement of Infantino in September and proposed to seek ways to transform how Fifa is run.

In a recent development, "A project with such a significant impact on the future of football could not be envisaged without comprehensive information, in-depth consultation and a fully transparent decision-making process," FFF president Philippe Diallo stated in a statement, who is now running against Infantino as Uefa’s last-minute candidate. "Fifa's governance does not live up to the standards that football represents.".

The Georgian Football Federation similarly withdrew its support for Infantino’s candidacy.

The German federation (DFB) already opted against endorsing Infantino earlier in the year so has not had to send a letter withdrawing support to take an opposing stance.

In a recent development, “The DFB has not signed a letter of support for the re-election of Gianni Infantino," the governing body stated in July. "Further steps will be discussed in the DFB presidential board.".

Former Germany national team director Oliver Bierhoff further reiterated the nation’s loss of trust in Infantino: "We have to take care of football. It is already commercial but it is a property for all of football. The world views may be different but in the last weeks and months a lot happened so that we have no trust any more that it will be going in the right direction.".

Another smaller footballing nation to withdraw its endorsement, Gibraltar aligned itself with Uefa.

“Accordingly, the Gibraltar FA has decided that it can no longer maintain its endorsement of Mr Infantino’s candidature for the 2027 Fifa presidential election. Fifa has been formally informed of that decision,” a statement read.

The Greek Football Association has backed Uefa’s push for a change in Fifa’s leadership, similarly withdrawing support to underscore a united European front in opposition to Infantino.

Recent findings suggest that "The Greek FA (EPO) has taken a clear position against a candidacy of Gianni Infantino," EPO presdient Makis Gagatsis told reporters. "We saw things happen at the World Cup that are not acceptable to football public opinion. Then... came a programme to sell World Cup rights and we are clearly against it, so we withdrew our support of the Fifa president.".

Part of the Nordic collective against the incumbent president, Iceland have also lost confidence in Infantino.

The Israel Football Association was another to formally send a letter to Fifa withdrawing its endorsement of Infantino’s re-election.

In his letter, FA president Moshe Zuares notes there was an “unprecedented crisis of confidence” between the visions of Uefa and Fifa when it comes to global governance, adding that the rift is “profound, substantive, and principled, and compelling all stakeholders to reconsider the path forward”.

The Italian Football Federation (FIGC) initially delayed taking official action but it has now withdrawn its support for Infantino's candidacy in the next Fifa presidential election scheduled.

"This decision is intended to clearly and transparently express the FIGC's position - in full agreement with Uefa and its president Aleksander Ceferin - regarding the recent initiatives promoted by the FIFA president concerning the governance and development of international competitions," FIGC mentioned in a statement.

The Football Association of Montenegro has withdrawn its support for Gianni Infantino’s bid for another term.

“The proposals that have been put forward, as they assessed, have exposed worrying vulnerabilities in terms of governance, not only at the political level but also within the administration,” a statement read. “Therefore, the Football Association of Montenegro has decided to withdraw its letter of support, previously given in favour of Mr Gianni Infantino’s candidacy for re-election in 2027.”.

The Royal Dutch Football Association (KNVB) is among the many to have confirmed it has lost confidence in Infantino’s leadership.

According to recent reports, “The way this process has unfolded has resulted in a fundamental loss of confidence in the leadership of Fifa President Gianni Infantino. The KNVB no longer has confidence in his leadership,” a statement read.

The Northern Irish football association (IFA) has expressed “concerns” over Infantino’s leadership.

"We take our responsibilities as a member association of both Uefa and Fifa seriously," said an IFA spokesperson. "We support the current Uefa position on the matter and will continue to engage constructively on issues relating to football governance. We are of course aware of the recent developments and wider concerns within the football community. We are considering these matters carefully and will continue to engage through the appropriate governance structures and channels.”.

The Norwegian Football Federation (NFF) have been one of the most vocal bodies to call for Infantino’s resignation.

Recent findings suggest that NFF president Lise Klaveness told the Guardian: “We decided that there is no trust in Infantino now. We have been worried consistently and there has been one more step in worrying direction every year, every part of the year. The trust is now gone for us, there is no way back for Infantino.

“We’re left in a very polarised cooperation globally and, I would say, chaos. So we will ask him to resign immediately so that the global football community can look ahead and cooperate going into the future.”.

The Football Association of Ireland (FAI) has followed in withdrawing its support for Infantino while backing Uefa’s stance.

Sources indicate that "Following an FAI board meeting, the decision was taken to rescind the letter of support that the Association supplied earlier this year," it confirmed. "It has since written to Fifa to explain its reasoning. The Association is grateful for the support that Fifa provides to Irish football, but recent events have raised significant concerns regarding governance, transparency and the lack of meaningful consultation.”.

The Romanian Football Federation (FRF) was among the countries to resolutely reject the sell-off proposal, calling it “a dangerous initiative to turn football into a private asset”.

As a result, the FRF will withhold support for Infantino’s re-election for the time being, with a statement reading: “FRF is suspending the discussion regarding the support of Fifa President Gianni Infantino for a new term, until further clarifications.”.

The SFA’s chief executive Ian Maxwell told the BBC that the governing body’s position has “been clear” since Uefa’s collective statement.

In a recent development, he noted: “We have aligned ourselves with the Uefa position and 55 nations are stronger than one voice. Their statement since then has talked about a lack of confidence in the Fifa leadership and the Scottish FA agree completely with that decision. The SFA will not be voting for Gianni Infantino come the re-election in early 2027.”.

The Football Association of Serbia sent a similar letter withdrawing support to Fifa.

“We would like to remind you that we provided our support to Mr Infantino in writing on 25 May of this year, but after carefully considering the events that have seriously damaged the image and reputation of both Fifa and its president in the past period, this is the only logical and rational course of action,” a statement read.

Sweden’s federation (SvFF) followed suit: "At an extraordinary board meeting on Monday, SvFF has chosen not to support Fifa President Gianni Infantino ​in the upcoming re-election.

Recent findings suggest that "This is after a long-term assessment of the development within Fifa and the organization's leadership. The decision is based on recurring shortcomings in governance, transparency and management, which means that trust in Gianni Infantino's leadership no longer exists.".

The Swiss Football Association (SFV) withdrew its backing of Infantino’s bid for another term as Fifa president at the end of September, saying it “cannot justify continuing to support Gianni Infantino’s candidacy”.

Their former international captain Ramon Vega is challenging Infantino.

The Football Association of Wales was one of the first to send its letter withdrawing support for Infantino.

Recent findings suggest that “The ‌recent failures in good governance, processes, ‌leadership, values, stakeholder management, communications and sound judgment ​have led us to a position ‌where Mr Infantino has lost the confidence of the FAW to ‌remain at the helm of world football,” a statement read. “Failing to put the best interests of football first is a failure we cannot accept.”.

The United States joined forces with Canada to call for “meaningful change that strengthens Fifa’s governance, transparency and accountability”.

Same as above, with Canadian prime minister Mark Carney stating that he no longer has confidence in Infantino.

Sources indicate that “It should be fatal,” Carney said following Infantino’s botched sell-off plan. “Certainly I don’t have confidence in Mr. Infantino.".

It has been revealed that the Japanese Football Federation (JFA) are backing their own candidate for president, with Kozo Tashima challenging Infantino. This signifies a rupture in Asia’s collective backing of Infantino, with Tashima confirming he already has at least five member associations backing him on the continent.

Asked about his ‌objectives, the 68-year-old Tashima said: "First and foremost, I believe it is essential to establish proper governance and ensure that transparency is firmly maintained.

According to recent reports, "We must get that right first. Then, on top of that, various policies can be put forward.".

Jordan were the first non-Uefa member association to publicly oppose Infantino after federation president Prince Ali bin Hussein levelled accusations of blackmail against Fifa.

Industry observers note that prince Ali alleged the organisation offered assistance with the kingdom's challenges in exchange for his endorsement, following Infantino's withdrawal from a World Cup stake sale proposal. Among the problems cited was the association's eight-month wait for prize money, due since December for reaching the Arab Cup final in Qatar.

After taking to X to reveal the outstanding payments, the Jordan Football Association received the prize money two days later - but Prince Ali has not changed his stance over not endorsing Infantino: “It does not change my clear position concerning the leadership of Fifa: my FA and I will not endorse president Infantino, nor will we vote for him.”.

Latest Zealand have broken rank with Oceania’s confederation by withdrawing their support for Infantino.

"After careful consideration, NZF has formed the view that decisions and actions within Fifa have contributed to a breakdown in trust and increased division within international football, and that an independent review is required to restore confidence and trust,” a statement read.

Confederation of African Football (54 members) 🌍.

Caf, the governing body for African football, was the first confederation to unanimously back Infantino.

“We are committed to continue working together with Fifa, its member associations, other football confederations and stakeholders to safeguard and adhere to governance, due process, and transparency global best practises and to contribute to the development and growth of football worldwide,” Caf president Patrice Motsepe said.

Motsepe later added that the position of embattled president Infantino can only be decided by Fifa elections.

Asian Football Confederation (47 members) 🌏.

The Asian Football Confederation (AFC) has endorsed Infantino in an apparent turnaround in its stance from two months ago when it criticised the head of football’s world governing body for a breach of trust.

AFC president Sheikh Salman bin Ibrahim Al Khalifa, speaking at the body’s extraordinary congress meeting in Tokyo on Friday, embraced Infantino with a large hug in front of the membership as he delivered his endorsement.

It has been revealed that “We affirm our full commitment to supporting you and your leadership as you seek a latest mandate as the Fifa president.” Sheikh Salman stated. “You’ve visited a lot of countries in Asia. I’ve spoken to a lot of members within this continent. I know your feeling and I think your commitment is clear as well.”.

South American governing body Conmebol, with its 10 member associations, expressed “concern about the repeated unilateral actions taken” and welcomed the decision to withdraw the plans, affirming it will “not support any action” that “ignores or deviates” from the “democratic procedures that represent the 211 Fifa member associations”.

Sources indicate that but having already endorsed Infantino in the summer, it appears they have stuck with their stance and not wavered as one of the Swiss-Italian’s firmest strongholds. Reports state that Conmebol “maintains its support for Infantino”, with an official statement set to be made following its meeting in Barranquilla on 20 November.

Caribbean Football Union (25 members) 🌎.

Following a pair of visits to the Caribbean, the CFU revealed on Friday that it will endorse Infantino for another term. This is despite Concacaf, the governing body of North America and the Caribbean, being in opposition.

Industry observers note that “The CFU emphasizes that it determined its collective position through consultation with its member associations,” the organisation said in a statement. “In this same spirit the CFU continues to call for increased transparency, good governance, and meaningful reform within the football family.”.

Uefa is not fully unified in its opposition of Infantino, with Azerbaijan one of two nations to publicly back the incumbent president.

“The Association of Football Federations of Azerbaijan (AFFA) fully supports Fifa and Fifa President Gianni Infantino,” a statement read after a visit to Hovsan.

Similarly, the association of Latvia has stood in support of Infantino amid criticism from Uefa.

Recent findings suggest that “Gianni Infantino does so many things that it is difficult to list in one minute, but I am grateful for his support around the world, his contribution to the development of football, and, of course, Latvia is always on his side,” mentioned federation president Vadims Lyashenko. “He can count on our support.”.

Benin’s federation looks set to back Infantino in next March’s election.

“I see no reason not to support him,” mentioned Mathurin de Chacus, president of the Benin federation.

FA president Alexandre Muyenge of Burundi echoed the remarks by his Benin counterpart supporting Infantino.

It has been revealed that he stated: “He is a president who is doing what is necessary to support Africa, particularly the less wealthy countries. His record is good, so it is logical to support him.".

The president of the Comoros Football Federation, Noted Ali Athouman, backed Infantino’s scheme due to the financial benefits to smaller nations.

"Our problem is how to obtain money,” he remarked. “Right now, we have no sponsors. So how do we compete? The richest nations can train players, have infrastructure and equipment, and it's no coincidence that they then achieve results. Most European countries don't have ​these problems.”.

The Djiboutian Football Federation has similarly welcomed the decision to withdraw the sell-off proposal, with president Souleiman Hassan Waberi saying the climbdown “demonstrates a firm commitment to preserving the unity, solidarity and cohesion that define the football family”.

He noted in a statement: “I reaffirm my full support for Fifa President Mr Gianni Infantino and for all initiatives aimed at promoting the sustainable, transparent and inclusive development of football around the world.”.

DR Congo's federation (Fecofa) president Veron Mosengo-Omba, who was only elected in May, spoke out in “full support” of Infantino. The two studied at university in Switzerland together.

Fecofa stated it had "greatly benefited" from Fifa's programmes, citing investment in development and infrastructure.

Egypt have maintained their endorsement of Infantino, similar to heir North African counterparts.

"The Egyptian Football Association reiterates its full trust in President Gianni Infantino's leadership and its continuous support for any initiatives that benefit Fifa member associations and the future of world football,” a statement read.

Lamin Kaba Bajo told BBC Sport that his federation not just stood by Infantino, but would do "everything within our means" to get him re-elected.

"That's my personal opinion as president of the federation, and a good number of African memberships also stand on that line. He is here to stay,” he said.

Fleetwood Haiya, Malawi's football chief, cited the nation’s financial concerns in why he supported Infantino.

In a recent development, he told BBC Sport: "Our government is not able to make sure that they have medical supplies in hospitals and at the same time to look at football. Malawi needs money.".

Ahmed Yahya, the country's representative on the Fifa Council, was one of a number of African football leaders to say he was backing Infantino early on, pledging his support before Caf took its stance.

The location of Infantino’s initial crisis meeting back in the summer, Morocco have stuck by the Swiss-Italian as one of his most loyal allies.

“What has been achieved in recent years through Fifa’s development programmes, particularly in Africa, represents an key accomplishment that must be preserved, to the benefit of all member associations,” said the Royal Moroccan Football Federation’s president Fouzi Lekjaa.

Like Mauritania, Hamidou Djibrilla from Niger came out promptly in support of Infantino.

The Nigeria Football Federation (NFF) has largely aligned itself towards a supportive stance for Infantino's leadership, with former NFF president and deputy chairman of Fifa's Men's National Teams Competitions Committee, Amaju Pinnick, backing his initial sell-off plan.

Namibia Football Association president Robert Shimooshili has backed Infantino and reiterated that his federation stands with Caf.

Industry observers note that “If CAF rallies behind Infantino, then we also support the president of Fifa at the moment. We have confidence in him, and we don’t mind what Uefa or AFC or Concacaf say. That is their right and we cannot do anything about it,” he said.

Sudan’s federation joined five other Arab nations - Qatar, Lebanon, Morocco, Egypt and Mauritania - in writing a joint statement backing Infantino.

Sources indicate that "Recognising the key role of Arab football in bringing people together and strengthening co-operation among football associations across the Arab world, we ... express our full support for Mr Gianni Infantino, president of Fifa, and reaffirm our confidence in his leadership and continued commitment to the development of football worldwide," the statement read.

In a recent development, "We deeply appreciate Mr Infantino’s sustained efforts to advance football globally, expand opportunities across all regions and strengthen the game’s role in bringing people and communities together. We look forward to continuing our close cooperation with him towards a stronger and more prosperous future for world ‌football, expanding opportunities and further enhancing Arab football’s contribution to ​the global game.".

While not an official statement from the federation, South Africa’s Minister of Sports, Arts and Culture of South Africa, Gayton McKenzie, posted on X saying that Infantino had been "very good to African football".

"Africa should be cautious in joining the public lynching of Infantino,” he warned. “He has been very good to African football. We can debate his ideas but let's not forget who has been a friend to us. Many of those calling for his head want the old status quo back too.".

The Ugandan federation are noted to have echoed the sentiments of Malawi and comoros, with football officials from the federation telling BBC Sport that Fifa investment has transformed their game both on and off the pitch.

The Bhutan Football Federation has published a letter that extends its “sincere appreciation” to Infantino for scrapping the plans, hailing him for demonstrating “true leadership” by “prioritising consensus over commerce”.

“We stand united with Fifa and President Infantino in their ongoing efforts to serve the global football community,” wrote federation president Dasho Ugen Tsechup.

Like others, Kuwait welcomed the decision to halt the plans but Sheikh Ahmed Yusuf Al-Sabah, the president of the Kuwait Football Association, affirmed his support for Infantino.

A statement read: “He concluded by affirming the Kuwait Football Association's confidence in the leadership of Fifa President Gianni Infantino, and its support for efforts aimed at developing the game and enhancing its opportunities for growth in a way that serves all national associations and achieves the shared interests of global football.”.

Lebanon, who granted Infantino citizenship last year, have backed the Swiss-Italian, with FA president Hashim Haidar all but echoing the same sentiments as Kuwait.

In a recent development, “Haidar reaffirms the Lebanese Football Association’s support for Fifa President Gianni Infantino and his confidence in the decisions he makes in the best interests of global football, as well as in his efforts and initiatives aimed at developing the game,” he remarked, while also asserting that Infantino’s proposal “could be re-examined ... in a away that serves the greater good of the sport and preserves its unity”.

The president of the Indonesian FA supported Infantino’s sell-off blueprint and has now backed him for another term.

Hailing Fifa as a “strategic partner that is truly present” in its football development, Erick Thohir said: “This is proof of President Infantino’s vision that football development must not be centered on a single region; it must proceed worldwide.”.

The Mongolian Football Federation has likewise put out a statement in support of Infantino.

Qatar was the first football association to publicly back Infantino during his attempts to sell off the World Cup, even though they later welcomed the decision to scrap the strategy.

"While the proposal had merit, we applaud the wisdom behind prioritising unity among member associations. The Qatar Football Association fully supports President Infantino's efforts to continue growing and strengthening the game globally,” a statement read.

Philippines have also backed Infantino and called for co-operation among confederations.

"We stand behind President Gianni Infantino's leadership, and trust that continued dialogue among all confederations and member associations will keep the global game moving forward together,” the Philippines confirmed.

Saudi Arabia, the controversial host of the 2034 World Cup, unsurprisingly came out in support of Infantino in the fallout of the scandal.

"At this time, SAFF supports the continued efforts ​of Fifa President Gianni Infantino and Fifa’s leadership to restore unity across ⁠the football family and continue growing the game for the benefit of all," ​the federation noted in a statement on its website.

Like Qatar, Sri Lanka welcomed the decision to scrap the investment blueprint and has since reaffirmed its support for Infantino.

"One of President Infantino's defining leadership qualities has always been his willingness to listen to the views and concerns of Member Associations. This decision is a clear reflection of his inclusive leadership style, built on dialogue, mutual respect, and a genuine commitment to serving the global football community," its statement read.

The UAE Football Association backed Infantino after Fifa withdrew its proposed private investment blueprint, with president Sheikh Hamdan bin Mubarak Al Nahyan saying the FA “reaffirmed its confidence” in his leadership.

Argentina became the first member from South America to voice its support for Infantino, on the same day that confederation Conmebol - which had previously only expressed backing of Infantino - expressed concern over Fifa’s procedures.

"Of our highest consideration, on behalf of the Argentine Football Association (AFA), and its Executive Committee, we address you, dear President, and through your worthy intermediary the Fifa board, to express our support for the management carried out during the last 10 years, which had as its main axes the development of football throughout the world and institutional solidity based on a clear governance model, stable and transparent,” a statement read.

The Ecuador federation (FEF) welcomed the proposal’s withdrawal and expressed confidence in Infantino’s leadership.

“We trust that you, and those who are at the moment leading football, will continue working for the benefit of our sport,” read the statement.

Paraguay also followed suit as Infantino’s Conmebol support base surfaced.

Their federation published a letter of support addressed to Infantino, writing that it "reaffirms its commitment to continue working alongside Fifa”.

Venezuela was another from South America to publicly support Infantino.

“We reiterate our commitment to continue working shoulder to shoulder under your leadership and with the other sister associations to promote the massification and excellence of all modalities of our discipline,” read a statement from the federation.

One of the many island nations to break away from Concacaf is Antigua and Barbuda, with the Caribbean being re-established as an Infantino stronghold.

Sources indicate that “[Infantino’s] transformative policies, from ground-breaking investment in grassroots infrastructure to the historic expansion of World Cup access, have elevated the aspirations of emerging football nations into attainable realities,” the ABFA noted in a statement. “By listening with genuine humility and acting with decisive conviction, he has forged a legacy of inclusivity that transcends the sport itself, affirming that every nation, regardless of size, deserves equal voice and fair opportunity on the world stage.”.

Another Caribbean federation to support Infantino’s leadership is the British Virgin Islands.

Industry observers note that BVI FA president Avanell Morton remarked: “Well, what more can he do? He’s doing a fantastic job already and doing a fantastic job for the entire region. It’s about football and as long as you are about football, then you have the opportunity to make football the priority.”.

Grenada’s federation (GFA) has also broken away from the Concacaf block and reaffirmed its support for Infantino.

“The GFA reaffirms its support for Fifa President Gianni Infantino and expresses its sincere appreciation for his continued support for football development in Grenada and across the Caribbean over his period of service in office and for the years to come,” a statement read.

JFF president Michael Ricketts has similarly reaffirmed his federation’s support in Infantino, breaking away from the Concacaf stance.

“I think Infantino has done so very well for football globally,” he said. “I remember when I got into football as the president, the support from Fifa was medial to say the least.It has been a lot better now and we are just very grateful and we are looking forward to further improvements so that we can impact not just football but the social well-being of every boy and girl who plays the sport.”.

Mexico is the only non-Caribbean Concacaf member to support Infantino, breaking away from the stance taken by its 2026 World Cup co-hosts, the United States and Canada.

The Mexican Football Federation (FMF) stated: "The FMF will neither recognise nor approve any process convened outside of that institutional framework, and it joins the call made... by President Infantino to collectively continue developing football for the benefit of the 211 member associations.".

The Saint Kitts and Nevis Football Association (SKNFA) has welcomed Infantino’s decision to scrap the plan, called for respect of Fifa’s institutional processes and backed the president to continue.

It stated: “The SKNFA concluded by reaffirming its support for Infantino’s leadership and vision, and said it looks forward to supporting him as he completes his current constitutional mandate and continues efforts to advance football development across Fifa’s 211 Member Associations.”.

One of just three Caribbean nations to ever qualify for a World Cup, Trinidad and Tobago president Kieron Edwards claims he has no doubts that the TTFA will back Infantino next year.

It has been revealed that “We would have given President Infantino our full support and we have not wavered with that. Things do come up, changes, you have to have discussions, you have to have dialogue but the support is there 100 per cent behind the President always,” he said.

With the Oceania Football Confederation yet to take an official stance, the Football Federation of American Samoa to come out on their own and back Infantino, sending a letter to the incumbent president to express “sincere gratitude for your outstanding leadership of the the Fifa family worldwide”.

Newly introduced Caledonia federation president Steeve Laigle has acknowledged Infantino’s “political mistake” but continues to defend the Fifa chief, whose World Cup expansion allowed the tiny Pacific island to reach a World Cup play-off.

Papua Newly introduced Guinea’s association (PNGFA) was quick to “reaffirm its full support for Fifa president Gianni Infantino” in the aftermath of his botched privatisation bid.

The Solomon Islands also expressed its “continued confidence in his leadership” in regards to Infantino’s presidency.

Tahiti are also remarked to have expressed their support before the OFC have taken an official stance.

The Oceania Football Confederation (OFC), with its 11 member associations, stopped short from pulling its support for Infantino in their statement after welcoming the scrapping of the sell-off strategy, very much staying on the fence as it called for a “review”.

A statement read: "The OFC recognises the progress achieved over the last decade in advancing football development in Oceania under Fifa's leadership and encourages Fifa to use the review as an opportunity to identify and implement any changes that may be necessary.".

Individual members of the confederation have already taken stances, as seen above.

Sources indicate that as things stand, The Independent tallies that Infantino has 142 member associations backing him for re-election, while 71 members are outwardly confirmed to be opposing him. This is taking into account the endorsements of confederations, which are being considered as a blanket vote from all members under that governing body unless a member has broken rank.

For example, Jordan’s opposition to Infantino means he is not included in the other 46 AFC member associations supporting Infantino, per the confederation’s endorsement, while the likes of Mexico, Jamaica, Trinidad and Tobago and more are all separate from the other Concacaf members in opposition.

Sources indicate that this suggests that Infantino is well on course for re-election. However, each nation has a vote for itself and some could go against their confederation’s stance. Japan’s decision to run a rival candidate signifies Asia is not unanimous with its support of Infantino, with Tashima having at least five other member associations backing him - something he will later reveal. Meanwhile, the Brazilian federation president publicly opposed Infantino’s sell-off looks and may not be aligned with Conmebol.

Nevertheless, there will need to be a massive swing from within Infantino’s strongholds if the tide is to turn against the Swiss-Italian come next March’s election.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, homo erectus might have also lived in rainforests — previously thought to be a habitat in which only modern humans could have thrived.Credit: S. Entressangle/E. Daynes/SPL.

Homo erectus is already one of humans’ most extraordinary ancient relatives. The big-brained, tool-wielding species emerged two million years ago in Africa and expanded across Eurasia, before vanishing around 100,000 years ago in Java, Indonesia.

Did Homo erectus and Denisovans mate? Tooth proteins hint at ancient trysts.

Recent findings suggest that did Homo erectus and Denisovans mate? Tooth proteins hint at ancient trysts.

Industry observers note that researchers have now added another feather to the hominin’s cap. A pair of studies analysing fossil teeth1,2, which were published in Nature on 18 November, suggest that H. erectus thrived in dense rainforests in southern China as recently as 180,000 years ago.

Researchers had thought that H. erectus was limited to savannahs and open woodlands, indicates Kira Westaway, a geochronologist at Macquarie University in Sydney, Australia, and a co-author of both studies.

Sources indicate that “Never, ever have we seen them in rainforests,” she adds. “This is a really major deal, because we thought Homo sapiens were the only species that had the skill set to survive in really challenging rainforest environments.”.

The earliest H. erectus fossils, from eastern Africa, are 1.9 million years old. But the svelte, upright-walking and running hominins wasted little time, reaching western Asia and present-day China some 200,000 years later and modern Java, using land bridges, not long after. The last-known H. erectus remains, from central Java, date to roughly 110,000 years ago3.

Limestone caves in Guangxi province, southern China, contained more than 10,000 fossil teeth.Credit: Kira Westaway (Macquarie University).

While looking for fossils from a three-metre-tall great ape called Gigantopithecus, Westaway and her colleagues identified a pair of limestone caves in Guangxi province in southern China. There, they discovered more than 10,000 fossil teeth from animals such as orangutans (Pongo spp.), monkeys and wild boar (Sus spp.), as well as 9 from hominins. The researchers estimate that the hominins lived between 184,000 and 324,000 years ago, according to dating of both fossils and the surrounding sediments using various methods.

In a recent development, eight of the hominin teeth resembled those of H. erectus in their shape, a designation that was confirmed by analysing the sequences of proteins preserved in the dental enamel of four specimens, says co-author Frido Welker, a molecular palaeoanthropologist at the University of Copenhagen.

The tooth enamel was analysed and its proteins sequenced.Credit: Kira Westaway (Macquarie University).

Recent findings suggest that the ninth lacked the shape and protein signature of H. erectus teeth, states Welker, and it also didn’t resemble those of H. sapiens or Neanderthals (Homo neanderthalensis). Denisovans — enigmatic ancient humans first discovered in southern Siberia and now linked to diverse fossils from China and elsewhere in Asia — are a possibility, but the evidence is circumstantial, says Welker. “Every label we put on that ninth tooth is a little bit of speculation.”.

The multitude of animal teeth was probably accumulated by a scavenger such as a porcupine. The presence of fossils from species such as muntjac deer (Muntiacus muntjac), leopards and orangutans hints at a rainforest environment.

  • It has been revealed that “The Scotland men’s team’s highest Fifa ranking was 13th (in 2007) and the worst was 88th place (in 2005) – a difference of 75 positions,” writes Bogdan Kotarlic.
  • Sources indicate that the gap between Scotland’s best and worst Fifa rankings isn’t the biggest in men’s international football; in fact, Pete Tomlin calculates that a 75-place swing puts them joint 141st with Ghana and Seychelles.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Plus: clubs with roads on their team badges, most and fewest managers per league title, and more.

Mail us with all of your questions and answers.

It has been revealed that “The Scotland men’s team’s highest Fifa ranking was 13th (in 2007) and the worst was 88th place (in 2005) – a difference of 75 positions,” writes Bogdan Kotarlic. “Is this the biggest gap between the best and worst ranking for one national team?”.

Sources indicate that the gap between Scotland’s best and worst Fifa rankings isn’t the biggest in men’s international football; in fact, Pete Tomlin calculates that a 75-place swing puts them joint 141st with Ghana and Seychelles. And, as Chris Lewis and others point out, there are a couple of other home nations who have had more dramatic swings. Wales and Northern Ireland both moved up 109 places: Wales from 117th to eighth under Gary Speed and then Chris Coleman, Northern Ireland from 129th in 2004 to 20th in 2017.

It is the speed of Scotland’s improvement that was most notable. “At two years, seven months and one day that feels like quite the rise,” writes Robbie Dale. “A look at the data shows it is bettered by only nine other countries. Colombia’s rise from a low of 51 to a high of 12 in exactly two years [between 2016 and 2018] is one notable example. Dominica and Kenya rose up the ranks by 70 and 69 places respectively over the course of just 16 months.”.

Industry observers note that some of the biggest movers are countries who joined Fifa after the men’s rankings were introduced in 1992, which means they started at the bottom. “I immediately thought of Bosnia and Herzegovina,” writes JJ Galbraith. “They were ranked 173rd in 1996, shortly after playing their first game as an independent nation. Their pinnacle was 13th place in 2013 – a rise of 160 places.”.

Sources indicate that that 160-place gap is beaten by only two teams. Kuwait reached 24th in the Fifa rankings in 1998, when they won the Arabian Gulf Cup in style and finished second at the Asian Games. By 2017 they were 189th in the world, a difference of 165 places.

That is 18 places short of the record. “Montenegro were ranked 199th when they played their first international match in 2007,” writes Pete Tomlin. “In 2011 they managed to climb up to 16th, thanks to some strong results in Euro 2012 qualifying (victories against Wales, Bulgaria and Switzerland and a 0-0 draw with England at Wembley).”.

Thanks to Pete, Mark Holt, Cameron McGlone, Sean DeLoughry and others for helping us compile this list of the biggest movers.

183 places Montenegro (16th/199th).

160 Bosnia and Herzegovina (13/173).

153 Central African Republic (49/202).

136 Cuba (46/182), Slovakia (14/150).

Industry observers note that pete Tomlin has also crunched the numbers for the women’s game. “The gaps are much smaller,” writes Pete, “due to the fact that the rankings have only been recorded since 2003, there are fewer teams and many of the national sides play very few matches.

Industry observers note that “The biggest gap belongs to the Bahamas with a high of 96th and a low of 194th, a difference of 98 places. There are actually two women’s teams with a gap of zero, but this is because they have played so few games. Chad (156th) and Sudan (194th) have never moved.”.

According to recent reports, “Non-league minnows Plymouth Parkway reached the second round of the FA Cup the other weekend,” writes Jon Archer. “I noticed their club crest appears to feature a road going under a bridge. Are there any other clubs who have roads on their badge?” Indeed the Southern League Premier Division South side have the A38 on their crest, a nod to, erm, the nearby stretch of dual carriageway that helps give the club its name via their former ground at the Parkway Sports Club.

Recent findings suggest that it is not a common occurrence and somewhat depends on how far you want to stretch things. Sunderland, for example, have a section of the Wearmouth Bridge on their crest, which certainly carries a road, though it is not visible. Similarly National League South’s Maidenhead United redesigned their badge in 2020 to celebrate the club’s 150th anniversary – it features a stretch of the town’s Thames river bridge, a nod to where the club played their first game back in 1870, which now carries the A4. Farther afield the German minnows TSG Backnang’s crest features the Murr Valley viaduct, which both overlooks the team’s ground and carries the B14, which links Stuttgart and Nuremberg.

Those might be a bit of a reach, but, far more definitively, across the West Country from Plymouth Parkway are tiny eighth-tier Willand Rovers of the Southern League Division One South. Their badge is a proper old shield effort featuring the River Culm, a castle tower … and the M5 motorway, which slices through the village to the north.

“Manchester United have 20 league titles, won by three managers. Liverpool have 20 league titles won by 10. Which teams have the most and fewest titles won by the most and fewest managers?” asks Will Marquand.

The answers above put Liverpool on two titles per manager and their great rivals down the M62 on 6.66 titles per manager (which is doing Alex Ferguson a great disservice but we have to find a way to make this question work). Daz Pearce offers up one-title-one-manager wonders Leicester (Claudio Ranieri), Nottingham Forest (Brian Clough) and Ipswich (Alf Ramsey) for the most managers per title. We would need a team winning only one title in their history in a season with two different managers to get lower than 1:1 but Dirk Maas has a more impressive example of a team with one manager per title.

“Since the inception of the Eredivisie in 1956, Feyenoord have secured 11 league titles, won by 11 managers: Jiri Sobotka in 1961, Franz Fuchs in 1962, Wilhelm Kment in 1965, Ben Peeters in 1969, Ernst Happel in 1971, Wiel Coerver in 1974, Thijs Libregts in 1984, Willem van Hanegem in 1993, Leo Beenhakker in 1999, Giovanni van Bronckhorst in 2017 and Arne Slot in 2023.” Alex Ferguson’s haul of 13 league titles over his 26 years in the Manchester United dugout makes United’s titles-per-manager ratio hard to beat and, probably, the definitive answer for fewest managers per title. Rangers have won 55 Scottish league titles with only nine managers for 6.11 titles per manager. That is as close as we could get. If you know of a club with a higher number of titles per manager, get in touch at knowledge@theguardian.com.

In a recent development, “It dawned on me recently that if Chelsea were to go on and win the Europa League this year on 15 May that, for a period of 10 days, they would be the holders of both major European trophies (as well as being technically the holders of the Cup Winners’ Cup),” wrote Brian Quinn in March 2013. “Has there ever been another brief period like this when a team held two European honours simultaneously? Perhaps going back to when there were three distinct European competitions?”.

Recent findings suggest that chelsea will indeed claim a unique honour if they triumph at the Amsterdam Arena in May (spoiler alert: they did). Only four sides have ever won different European competitions in consecutive years – Juventus, Milan, Porto and Liverpool – and in each instance the teams were deposed as holders of one trophy before getting their hands on the other.

It has been revealed that milan won the much-missed Cup Winners’ Cup on 23 May 1968, but Slovan Bratislava were crowned the upcoming champions on 21 May 1969, seven days before Milan hammered Ajax in the Bernabéu to win the 1969 European Cup. Similarly Juventus won the Cup Winners’ Cup on 16 May 1984, but Everton won that tournament almost exactly a year later on 15 May 1985, a fortnight before Juventus won the European Cup in a final overshadowed by the Heysel tragedy.

Likewise, Porto fell a week short in 2002-03 and 2003-04 after winning the Uefa Cup then the Champions League under José Mourinho, as did Liverpool between their Uefa Cup and European Cup wins in 1975-76 and 1976-77.

“Ronaldinho played for Ravenna, in Serie C, on Sunday. It was his first professional appearance in more than 11 years,” writes George Jones. “Have any other footballers had long career hiatuses? And has any player had a longer hiatus than 11 years?”.

“Against the Netherlands this week, Florian Wirtz scored one goal that went in off a post and one that went in off the crossbar. Has anyone ever gone one better and scored a hat-trick with a goal off each post and one off the crossbar?” wonders David Hagan.

Recent findings suggest that “Seeing Cuba thrash Grenada 9-0 in the Concacaf Nations League, I noted there were eight different scorers (Jorge Aguirre scoring twice). Has any team gone better?” asks Oliver Tuhey.

Recent findings suggest that “My team, Tranmere Rovers, have appeared at Wembley nine times since 1990,” writes David Carruthers. “Can any other team never to have played in the top division beat this?”.

“Are Leicester City the quickest team ever to go from winning the FA Cup to playing in the FA Cup first round proper?” asks Ricardio Sentulio.

Mail us with all of your questions and answers.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Shania Twain is standing up for others in country music.

The legendary star in the genre used her acceptance speech for the Equal Play Award at Sunday’s CMT Awards to call for more equity and diversity in the country music industry.

Recent findings suggest that “When I wrote the phrase ‘Man I feel like a woman’ I honestly had no idea at the time it would become an undercurrent of a decades-long career,” she stated, referring to one of her biggest hits. “It’s amazing how one statement can empower so many.”.

The phrase, Twain said, “has been adopted by an array of fantastic communities all around the world and become a genuine path of power…which brings me so much joy.”.

“I believe in an all-inclusive country music. We’re family,” Twain mentioned. “This is a genre of music with a rich history that raised and nurtured my own songwriting and performance and recording career from childhood. Currently, the industry standard does a real disservice to this.”.

Twain, who was presented the award by rapper Megan Thee Stallion, shouted out some of the diverse acts she is spotlighting on her “Queen of Me” tour this year, including Lily Rose, Lindsay Ell, Hailey Whitters, Mickey Guyton and others.

It has been revealed that “I will continue to do my best as a trailblazer,” Twain said. “Together, let’s ensure all our fellow artists get equal play regardless of gender, age or race.”.

She also performed acappella with the African American singing group, The BoykinZ, while presenting an award onstage. Twain connected with the group, who are sisters and rising country stars, after Kelly Clarkson surprised them recently by bringing Twain out to meet them during an episode of Clarkson’s daytime talk show.

#1064. The last golden era of the Premier League is long gone: Why 2004-16 was the best of the Barclays

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1103 w)
📖 Baca

The last golden era of the Premier League is long gone: Why 2004-16 was the best of the Barclays

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1103 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fourfourtwo

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For the so-called “Best League in the World™”, it’s safe to say the Premier League is currently experiencing a full-blown existential crisis.
  • It has been revealed that the bombshell announcement of Manchester City’s guilt on all but one of their 115 charges has left the game feeling more hollow than ever before.
  • So with that, let’s cast our minds to a simpler, purer time, the much-fabled “Barclays era” of 2004 to 2016.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For the so-called “Best League in the World™”, it’s safe to say the Premier League is currently experiencing a full-blown existential crisis.

It has been revealed that the bombshell announcement of Manchester City’s guilt on all but one of their 115 charges has left the game feeling more hollow than ever before. Is there a title race? Who’s going down? What is real? Does any of this mean anything? Throw in the continued abomination that is VAR and more, and it’s all just a bit bleak.

So with that, let’s cast our minds to a simpler, purer time, the much-fabled “Barclays era” of 2004 to 2016.

While football didn’t start in 1992, the Premier League did and by the early-to-mid 2000s, it was reaching its apex as the blood and thunder of decades prior fused with the new-found flair and panache to create a near-perfect concoction.

Recent findings suggest that the current state of the English top-flight can be traced all the way back to the summer of 2003 with Roman Abramovich’s purchase of Chelsea. It was the moment the horse bolted and nothing has been the same since.

It has been revealed that however, at the time, it was all just a little bit exciting and things really picked up 12 months later when Jose Mourinho landed in West London, rightly claiming to be the “Special One”. The reigning European Cup winner was joined by Rafael Benitez, who came to Liverpool after incredible success with Valencia.

Suddenly, Sir Alex Ferguson and Arsene Wenger were no longer the only gunslingers in town. The “Massive Two” quickly became the “Big Four” as Mourinho romped to the league title - breaking numerous records - and Benitez amazingly won the Champions League. Istanbul and all that.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

The two Iberians changed so much in the English game. From how to set up a side to how to win the title - 4-4-2 and peaking after Christmas being swapped out for 4-3-3 and rapid-fast starts.

Sources indicate that liverpool’s fifth European Cup was significant for numerous reasons. It was their first in 21 years but also the first final featuring an English side in the 21st century. They had beaten Chelsea to get there, starting both an incredible rivalry between the clubs and managers, and a golden age for the Premier League.

Over the next four years, all of the then-”Big Four” made finals and there were three semi-finalists in every season from 06/07 to 08/09. The peak came in 2008 when each was knocked out by another with United eventually toppling Chelsea in the first all-English final in Moscow. In one of the odder paradoxes, England failed to qualify for the European Championships that summer.

Fergie’s empire had struck back with Cristiano Ronaldo and Wayne Rooney at the forefront of it. In an era of elite pairings, there was no finer. Ronaldo’s Ballon d’Or win confirmed his status as the best player in the world, and the Premier League as truly the best league.

It was also a time of far less financial disparity with the rest of Europe, Milan and Inter lifting the Champions League in 2007 and 2010 respectively. Things would soon change and not for the better.

While the substantial boys competed for the biggest trophies, there were plenty of brilliant stories elsewhere. Harry Redknapp’s Portsmouth won the FA Cup in 2008, setting the tone for Wigan five years later in epic fashion against City months on from Swansea claiming the League Cup. Only Crystal Palace's success in 2025 has been comparable since.

Throw in Major Sam’s Bolton, Blackburn, Stoke, Hull and others and it was the last definitive age of the cult teams and cult heroes, or as they’ve become better known - The Barclaysmen. With the overload of data nowadays, another Michu-like madness feels further away than ever.

Abu Dhabi’s takeover of City in 2008 is the obvious place to pinpoint the beginning of the end, but Mourinho’s first Chelsea exit a year prior and Ronaldo’s first from United a year after moved the centre of attention from England to Spain.

According to recent reports, while European success faded - a fate-like Chelsea were the only winners from 2008 to 2019 - there were still memorable domestic moments, two of which unfortunately led to City winning their first pair of Premier League titles. Agueroooooo and Gerrard’s slip may be rendered utterly irrelevant soon but the memories won’t. It was peak Premier League.

As was Sir Alex Ferguson’s last dance in 2013 and Leicester’s miracle title win in 2016, which will never be topped as the greatest achievement in the history of English football. That it came either side of Chelsea’s crooked titles and prior to City’s dodgy dominance makes it all the more appropriate as the ending of the last great era. And that goes for both in football and the world itself.

While the on-field action of the last decade may feel fraudulent, how we now consume football is also a far cry from those halcyon Barclays days.

It has been revealed that streaming was not yet a thing in 2004. Sky Sports was in its pomp. Super Sunday actually lived up to its billing as appointment viewing.

Industry observers note that influencers and content creators had not yet taken over. Gary Neville went past his winger on the overlap rather than host it. Social media was still fun for the most part.

We had Soccer AM and Goals on Sunday, Gillette Soccer Saturday and Match of the Day at elite levels, and even room for reveals like Wayne Rooney’s Street Striker and Football’s Next Star.

Nostalgia is a helluva drug, but as Independent Panels decide the fate of English football past, present and future, it’s near-impossible to dispute that, like so much of entertainment, we had it so much better before.

One day, the pendulum will hopefully swing back in our favour but, for now, a rewatch of Premier League Years on Sky may be in order.

Peter writes freelance for FourFourTwo and has previous experience at Evening Standard and Football365 among several others. He now works for us alongside OneFootball, the Sporting News and Stats Perform. One of the very few Irish people living in London and even fewer to support Manchester United, he spends time away from football rewatching TV highlights and attempting to play tennis.

#1062. Breaking: ‘Pregnancy does not mean game over’: meet the footballers challenging the myths | Moving the Goalposts

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1180 w)
📖 Baca

Breaking: ‘Pregnancy does not mean game over’: meet the footballers challenging the myths | Moving the Goalposts

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1180 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theguardian

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Claire Emslie and Emma Kelly are among those taking advantage of upcoming research and guidelines for pregnant players.
  • Claire Emslie wasn’t expecting to be able to run at 81% of her max speed at 32 weeks pregnant.
  • Sources indicate that emslie, a Scotland international who also plays as a forward for Angel City FC, documented her journey through pregnancy and football training on social media and is part of a growing number of professional female footballers who are getting pregnant in their athletic prime and approaching motherhood with a fresh mindset.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Claire Emslie and Emma Kelly are among those taking advantage of upcoming research and guidelines for pregnant players.

Claire Emslie wasn’t expecting to be able to run at 81% of her max speed at 32 weeks pregnant.

Sources indicate that emslie, a Scotland international who also plays as a forward for Angel City FC, documented her journey through pregnancy and football training on social media and is part of a growing number of professional female footballers who are getting pregnant in their athletic prime and approaching motherhood with a fresh mindset. Rather than marking the end of a career (notably, Millie Bright revealed her pregnancy in September, months after having retired), pregnancy can mark both a continuation and a renewal.

Industry observers note that “I think it’s becoming more common. You’re seeing it more often, especially in America,” says 32-year-old Emslie, who trained at high intensity throughout her pregnancy, with a three-person team looking after her. She gave birth to her son, Jamie, in December 2025 and returned to competitive action by May 2026; scoring her first goal since coming back for Scotland in October, and her first club goal this month. “It’s amazing what the body can do. I debunked a lot of myths that I’d heard about being pregnant.”.

In a recent development, for many years, indicates the physiotherapist and Women’s Football Hub founder Carolyn Kent, there was huge caution around high-impact sports and pregnancy. The fear was that overexertion and physical contact – a heart rate going too high, a bad fall, a mistimed kick to the abdomen – could cause miscarriage. But slowly this is changing. In July Fifa introduced its Stay in Play guidelines and research, which offer a groundbreaking framework for decision-making around football participation during pregnancy.

According to recent reports, “I was always told that once you hit that first trimester, 12 weeks, all contact stops. But actually they’re now saying, no, we need to be a little bit more nuanced than that,” notes Kent. The research suggests that while that timeframe should still be considered the loose recommended cut-off point for full-contact football (due to the uterus growing over the pubic bone and offering less protection for the growing foetus in the second trimester), low-contact and modified training can continue in the absence of any medical reason for it not to.

Recent findings suggest that “Pregnancy does not mean game over,” adds Kent. “It does not mean that ‘OK, I’ve got to automatically stop’. That again feeds into this narrative that females are fragile. Your body’s amazing.”.

Industry observers note that up to 2021, only 6% of sports science research was done on women, which means gaps are still being filled in. But as the women’s game continues to grow, this is happening at speed, says Sinéad Dufour, a pelvic health physiotherapist and academic who was one of the researchers who developed the Stay in Play guidelines. She gives Fifa credit for recognising the development of the women’s game – its popularity and intensity has soared in the past 10 years with more than six million women and girls playing football in England alone.

“More and more players are now staying through until they’re having families … And they put all this money into research,” she claims. They have identified “clear cut” physical and mental health benefits for women to keep up with football, including a lower injury risk postpartum.

“There’s always been a notion that women just aren’t strong and robust the way we actually are, and now the science is proving otherwise,” Dufour says. “I do think some of it relates to the foetus. That’s going to supersede what’s actually good for the woman, right?”.

According to recent reports, some of the main considerations players should have, whether professional or amateur, as to whether they should keep playing and training throughout pregnancy, relate to pain, pelvic floor dysfunction, and motor control and movement, she adds. But the decision whether or not to continue playing during pregnancy is ultimately personal.

It has been revealed that when Emma Kelly, who plays for Newcastle, unexpectedly became pregnant earlier this year at the age of 29, she was anxious. She had never played with a pregnant teammate before and she had been out for much of the season due to injury. How isolating would the experience be? Was it going to jeopardise her career? “I was questioning whether this is the right time,” she says. “It’s not that I’m ungrateful but it’s just finding it hard being out of the team again and not being able to play the sport that I love.”.

Though she continued to train, she and her partner decided she would stop contact football immediately, prior to 12 weeks, as “football is so unpredictable”, she indicates. As she didn’t want to announce her pregnancy until she was into the second trimester, in the interim she told her teammates that she was unwell. Like Emslie she has been documenting her training with the encouragement of her club and feels as if she is noticing more and more athletes doing the same. “I want to continue as long as my body allows me to,” she says. Her club has been “extremely supportive” with specialised training, physio and equipment.

But for all the newfound positivity around pre-and postpartum for footballers, Emslie claims candidly, there are some hard truths that players have to face: namely that pregnancy is a sacrifice. The pitch is their stage and no player wants to be relegated to the role of understudy, relearning how to bend their body to their will. “If I wasn’t worried about [fertility], I wouldn’t have gotten pregnant till I was retired,” she says. “I could have had a full football career.”.

In a recent development, the other is that football is a business. “You’re used as a player,” she claims bluntly. “As soon as you turn a certain age, or if you’ve got a kid, they look at you different … As a player, you’re wanted until you’re not.” Though she made it clear she wasn’t talking about her own club, which was very supportive of her pregnancy and return, at the time of interview she was two months away from her contract ending with Angel City but had no news of a new deal being offered.

In a recent development, even so, Dufour says, the body works hard during pregnancy; aerobic capacity is pushed. “The biggest stress test you’re ever going to go through is pregnancy,” she says. Her data shows that some women will achieve personal bests on their return. In short pregnancy could be a secret superpower. In an industry as capitalistic, brutal and data-driven as football, that’s an crucial fact.

Andriy Shevchenko has accused Mykhailo Mudryk's representatives of trying to persuade the Ukrainian FA to find someone to falsely take the blame for the winger's failed drugs test.

Mudryk, now on loan at Tottenham from Chelsea, was suspended for 20 months between November 2024 and July 2026 after testing positive for banned substance meldonium in October 2024.

In an interview, Mudryk blamed the Ukrainian FA (UAF), claiming the substance entered his body while on international duty.

'This drug could only have got into my body where I was, and that's Ukraine,' he said.

It has been revealed that but Shevchenko, president of the UAF, described the accusations as 'baseless slander'. Shevchenko added: 'His representatives repeatedly approached the UAF with a proposal to find an employee who would falsely take responsibility for the meldonium found in his doping sample,' he told Tribuna. 'Such a proposal contradicts the principles of our work.'.

Industry observers note that shevchenko mentioned investigations had failed to establish how the substance entered Mudryk's system. He added that national team staff complied with Chelsea's request not to give Mudryk medication, and that two of his personal specialists were allowed at training camps.

Mykhailo Mudryk (left) has been accused of 'baseless slander' by Ukraine FA (UAF) president Andriy Shevchenko after he blamed his failed drugs test on the national team's setup.

'If Mykhailo has evidence to back up his words, let him provide it,' Shevchenko said, demanding a public retraction and apology otherwise.

Mudryk's representatives have been approached for comment.

In a recent development, the 25-year-old was initially handed a four-year ban after being charged by the Football Association for failing a doping test. He was able to return when a seismic resolution was struck after changes to the 'scientific reporting standards'.

In a bombshell two-hour interview with Ukrainian journalist Dmitry Gordon via his YouTube channel, Mudryk laid the blame for his situation with the Ukraine national team - something Shevchenko vehemently denies.

'Loud statements have been made about the UAF and the Ukrainian national team. This is baseless slander against our people, who do their work honestly and professionally,' the UAF president, who also played for Chelsea during his time, said in a statement to The Athletic.

'After Mykhailo became a Chelsea player, the club sent a letter to the UAF requesting that he not be given any medication during national team training camps,' he continued.

'The national team staff complied with this request. Head coach Serhiy Rebrov also approved for Mykhailo to have two of his personal specialists work with him at the training camps. These were the exact people who monitored his regimen and recovery, and helped him with his daily routine.

Mudryk has won 28 caps for Ukraine but is yet to represent them since his ban was overturned.

Recent findings suggest that 'The UAF completed all necessary checks in this case. We provided Mudryk's representatives with the information they requested and remained in contact with those working on the case.

'I know the people who have worked with the national team for many years. I trust them, because throughout all this time there have been no incidents in the team that could make anyone doubt their professionalism. If Mykhailo has evidence to back up his words, let him provide it. If no such evidence exists, I expect him to publicly retract his accusations and apologise to the people whose honesty and professionalism he has called into question.'.

In his interview, Mudryk - who is yet to add to his 28 caps for his country since returning from his ban - laid the blame at Ukraine's door.

According to recent reports, 'I had never heard of a drug like meldonium, never seen it, never come across it in my life. I only learned about it when they told me the news. I definitely have ideas. It's a drug you can only get in Eastern Europe,' the winger said.

'This drug could only have got into my body where I was, and that's Ukraine. There are no such drugs in England. It supposedly stimulates your heart and helps you, as far as I understand, handle physical load better.

Industry observers note that 'I was at home and Chelsea's management came to see me and they mentioned we needed to talk. Then they say you've returned a positive doping test and now you're facing a ban.

'You can't believe it's true. You can't believe this is happening to you. If I'd ever taken anything anywhere, I'd have understood that this conversation might happen one day.

He is currently on loan at Tottenham from Chelsea but has only played once so far this season.

According to recent reports, 'At least I'd have understood it was possible. But when you spend a huge pile of money on watching your diet, on a nutritionist, on a chef. When you spend that much money every year on all these things, that's the last thing you expect. Because it speaks for itself: that you take things very seriously, like nutrition, everything that goes into your body, you watch it very closely.

'Otherwise there'd be no need to spend money on it, because you could manage without it. They tell you this news, and you sit there, and you kind of listen to them but don't hear them.

'At some point you just go into a trance. It feels like you're falling in a dream off a skyscraper. You're flying down, you feel yourself flying down, and only in a dream do you wake up when you hit the ground, but in real life you don't wake up, you just keep falling. It hits you very hard mentally. At that moment the tears came later.'.

Mudryk, who joined Chelsea for £89million from Shakhtar Donetsk, has only made one substitute appearance for Tottenham so far this season due to an ankle injury.
